title: Git can undo almost anything: 4 commands
sources: git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog: reflogs record when branch tips and other refs were updated in the local repository; unreachable entries expire after gc.reflogExpireUnreachable, default 30 days (reachable: 90 days)
git-scm.com/docs/git-restore: restore paths in the working tree (from the index by default; --staged restores the index from HEAD)
git-scm.com/docs/git-stash: saves local modifications away and reverts the working directory to match HEAD; restore later with apply/pop
git-scm.com/docs/git-revert: records new commits that reverse the effect of earlier commits (history is not rewritten, so it is safe on pushed branches)
teyro.app: coding track, short daily lessons, real code with instant feedback, a few minutes a day

lines.text: You didn't lose that code. | Git *secretly* kept it.
Here are *four* commands | that undo almost *anything.*
The first is git *reflog.* | It's a diary of everywhere your branch has been, | so after a bad reset, | you find the old commit | and jump straight *back.*
By default, | Git keeps those lost commits | for *thirty days.*
The second is git *restore.* | Broke a file you haven't committed? | One command puts it back | the way it was *before* your edits.
The third is git *stash.* | Halfway through something | and need to switch branches? | Stash *parks* your changes, | and stash *pop* brings them back.
And finally, git *revert.* | Already pushed a bad commit to *GitHub?* | Don't rewrite history. | Revert adds a *new* commit that undoes it, | so nobody else's work *breaks.*
Reflog, restore, stash and revert. | That's your *undo* button.
If you want to practise real code like this, | a few minutes a day, | the link's in my *bio.* | It's called *Teyro.*
